reason: Attacked and not broken, and the verifier's correction is now on firmer ground than the verifier had. The weak point in the verdict was that its only full text of Boswell was Project Gutenberg 1564, which is not Boswell entire but Charles Grosvenor Osgood's ABRIDGEMENT (its own title page reads 'Abridged and edited, with an introduction'), so a hostile reading could say the card's wording was an abridger's normalisation. I therefore downloaded a second, independent and scholarly text, Project Gutenberg 8918, 'Life of Johnson, Volume 1', edited by George Birkbeck Norman Hill, and read the letter there. Hill prints, letter for letter: 'I hope it is no very cynical asperity not to confess obligations where no benefit has been received, or to be unwilling that the Publick should consider me as owing that to a Patron, which Providence has enabled me to do for myself.' Osgood agrees with Hill word for word. So all four discriminating readings the verdict turned on are confirmed twice over in two unrelated editions of Boswell: 'cynical' and not 'cinical', 'obligations' plural, 'Publick' in the old spelling with a capital, and 'Patron' and 'Providence' capitalised. The proposal's original 'obligation ... the Public' was indeed the wrong text. I then tested the verdict's other claim, that a rival family descends from the surviving manuscript copy: an Internet Archive full-text search for 'cinical asperity' returns 28 printed books, including the Huntington Library's 2009 Johnson exhibition catalogue and 'The Letters of Samuel Johnson', and every one of them reads 'cinical asperity not to confess obligation' with the singular. A search for 'no very cynical asperity not to confess obligation where' returns 65 more, the modernised hybrid. So two textual families really do exist, the card really does have to say which it quotes, and 'in Boswell, Life of Johnson' does say it, because the two Boswells I read agree. Locator: in Hill's text the letter body runs six paragraphs, 'MY LORD, I have been lately informed', 'When, upon some slight encouragement', 'Seven years, my Lord', 'The shepherd in Virgil', 'Is not a Patron, my Lord', 'Having carried on my work thus far', with the subscription after; the sentence stands in 'Is not a Patron, my Lord', which is the fifth of six and therefore the penultimate paragraph, as proposed and as verified. Date 7 February 1755 is the heading in both editions. Attribution is not in dispute and Johnson is on no line of the misattribution list; the letter is Johnson's, not Chesterfield's, and Chesterfield's own presence in the year at one line is no collision. Scope: correspondence by a named author, printed 1791, not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory, nothing needing a content warning; it is a rebuke but a courteous one, and at six in the morning it reads as the refusal to profess a gratitude one does not feel, which is the month's theme. shipped.js: shipped [], near [], person 'samuel johnson' yearCount 1 from month 3, cap 3, so a second line is allowed, not banned, not at cap; no second Johnson in the month's proposals and none among the June carry-ins. Mechanics: the source leads with the name, carries no dash, no straight double quote, and runs 101 characters, inside the cap; prose not broken into lines; ends in a full stop; tag Correspondence is the form of the work. One soft spot, not a refutation: the note says 'an edition has to be named' but the source line names only 'Boswell, Life of Johnson' and no editor. Having read Hill and Osgood side by side I am satisfied that naming Boswell is sufficient, because the difference the note cares about is between Boswell and the manuscript family, not between one Boswell and another; the note should be trimmed so it does not seem to promise an editor the source does not give.
